title: Operational Authority and Administrative Evolution of the Appropriate Officer of Customs
summary: The 'Appropriate Officer of Customs' functions as the primary operational authority under the Customs Act 1969, evolving from a broad statutory framework of enforcement powers into a role increasingly defined by digitized operational workflows, specific certification procedures, and standardized documentation.

evolution.scope: The scope remains consistent across the Act, covering the entire lifecycle of customs operations from arrival to clearance.
evolution.legal_basis: The legal basis is anchored in the 1969 Act, with procedural updates reflected in modern metadata forms.
evolution.procedure: Shift from general statutory authority to specific, documented operational workflows (e.g., container status remarks, industrial certification).

timeline.change: Establishment of the comprehensive legal framework defining the powers and duties of the Appropriate Officer.

static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
158. Power to search on reasonable ground.- (1) The appropriate officer, if he has reason to believe that any person is carrying about himself goods liable to confiscation or any documents relating thereto, may search such person, if he has landed from or is on board or is about to board a vessel within the 3[Bangladesh] customs-waters, or if he has alighted from or is about to get into or is in any other conveyance arriving in or proceeding from 3[Bangladesh] or if he is entering or about to leave 3[Bangladesh] or if he is within the limits of any customs-area.
(2) Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (1) the appropriate officer may search a person, if he has reason to believe that such person is carrying about himself smuggled Platinum, any radio active mineral, gold, silver, precious stones, manufactures of Platinum, any radio active mineral, gold, silver or precious stones, or currency, or any other goods or class of goods notified by the 4[Government] in the official Gazette, or any documents relating to any one or more of the aforementioned goods.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to search any person if there is a reasonable belief that the individual is carrying goods liable to confiscation or related documents.
The officer may conduct searches on persons located within customs-areas, in conveyances, or on vessels within Bangladesh customs-waters.
The officer has the authority to search persons suspected of carrying specific prohibited items like gold, silver, currency, or precious stones, or other goods notified by the Government.
Person: A person is subject to search by an appropriate officer if they are suspected of carrying goods liable to confiscation while present in customs-areas, or upon boarding or leaving vessels and conveyances.
Vessel: Vessels within the Bangladesh customs-waters serve as specific locations where an appropriate officer may exercise search powers over persons on board.
Conveyance: The appropriate officer is authorized to search persons arriving in or departing from Bangladesh who are in, alighting from, or entering into any conveyance.
Bangladesh customs-waters: This geographic area defines a zone where an appropriate officer may board and search vessels and the individuals located thereon.
Customs-area: The limits of a customs-area constitute a jurisdictional boundary within which the appropriate officer is granted the power to search persons.
Smuggled Goods: The search powers extend to persons suspected of carrying precious metals, minerals, stones, or currency, as well as any other goods specifically notified by the Government in the official Gazette.
Government: The Government has the authority to notify in the official Gazette specific classes of goods that, when carried by a person, provide grounds for a search by the appropriate officer.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Power to screen or X-Ray bodies of suspected persons for detecting secreted goods
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
160. Power to screen or X-Ray bodies of suspected persons for detecting secreted goods.- (1) Where the appropriate officer has reason to believe that any person liable to search under section 158 has any goods liable to confiscation secreted inside his body, he may detain such person and produce him without unnecessary delay before an officer of customs not below the rank of an 2[Assistant Commissioner of Customs].
(2) The aforesaid officer, if he has reasonable grounds for believing that such person has any such goods secreted inside his body and that it is necessary to have the body of such person screened or X-Rayed, may make an order to that effect, or else discharge such person forthwith, except where he is held on any other grounds.
(3) Where the aforesaid officer orders such person to be screened or X-Rayed, the appropriate officer shall, as soon as practicable, take him to a radiologist possessing such qualifications as may be recognised by the 3[Government] for that purpose and such person shall allow the radiologist to screen or X-Ray his body.
(4) The radiologist shall screen or X-Ray the body of such person and forward his report thereon, together with any X-Ray pictures taken by him to the aforesaid officer without unnecessary delay.
(5) Where on the basis of a report from a radiologist or otherwise, the aforesaid officer is satisfied that any person has any goods liable to confiscation secreted inside his body , he may direct that suitable action for bringing such goods out of his body be taken on the advice and under the supervision of a registered medical practitioner and such person shall be bound to comply with such direction:
Provided that in the case of a female no such action shall be taken except on the advice and under the supervision of a female registered medical practitioner.
(6) Where any person is brought before an officer of customs not below the rank of an 1[Assistant Commissioner of Customs] as aforesaid, he may direct that pending completion of all action under this section such person be detained.
(7) No person shall be subjected to screening or X-Ray if he confesses that goods liable to confiscation are secreted inside his body and of his own consent agrees to suitable steps being taken to bring out such goods.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is authorized to detain a suspected person if there is reason to believe they have secreted goods inside their body that are liable to confiscation.
The officer must promptly produce the detained person before an officer of at least the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs for further authorization of screening or X-ray procedures.
The officer is responsible for taking the suspect to a recognized radiologist for screening and must supervise or direct the removal of any secreted goods based on medical advice.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: A customs officer at or above the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs is authorized to review the case of a detained person and order a body screening or X-ray if reasonable grounds exist.
This officer is empowered to direct the detention of a suspect while the required medical actions or investigations are being completed.
Confiscated Goods: Goods suspected of being secreted inside a person's body and which are liable to confiscation are subject to detection through screening or X-ray procedures.
The law provides mechanisms for the recovery of such goods under medical supervision when their presence is confirmed.
Radiologist: A radiologist, possessing qualifications recognized by the Government, is the authorized professional tasked with performing body screenings or X-rays on suspects to detect secreted goods.
The radiologist is required to forward the screening report and any associated imagery to the relevant customs officer without delay.
Registered Medical Practitioner: Any action taken to remove secreted goods from a person's body must be performed under the advice and supervision of a registered medical practitioner.
In the case of a female suspect, the intervention must be supervised specifically by a female registered medical practitioner.
Government: The Government is responsible for recognizing the qualifications of the radiologists authorized to perform the medical procedures required for detecting secreted goods.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Power to stop and search conveyances
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
164. Power to stop and search conveyances.- (1) Where the appropriate officer has reason to believe that within the territories of 1[Bangladesh] (including territorial waters) any conveyance has been, is being, or is about to be used in the smuggling of any goods or in the carriage of any smuggled goods, he may at any time stop any such conveyance or, in the case of an aircraft, competent it to land, and-
(a) rummage and search any part of the conveyance ;
(b) examine and search any goods thereon ; and
(c) break open the lock f any door, fixure or package for making search.
(2) Where in the circumstances referred to in sub-section (1)-
(a) it becomes necessary to stop any vessel or compel any aircraft to land, it shall be lawful for any vessel or aircraft in the service of the Government while flying her proper flag or bearing flag marks and any authority authorised in this behalf by the 3[Government] to summon such vessel to stop or the aircraft to land, by means of an international signal, code or other recognised means, and thereupon such vessel shall forthwith stop or such aircraft shall forthwith land, and it fails to do so, chase may be given there to by any vessel or aircraft as aforesaid and if after a gun is fired as a signal the vessel fails to stop or the aircraft fails to land, it may be fired upon;
(b) it becomes necessary to stop any conveyance other than a vessel or aircraft, the appropriate officer may use or cause to be used all lawful means for stopping it or preventing it escape including, if all other means fail, firing upon it.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to stop and search any conveyance if they have reason to believe it is being used for smuggling goods or transporting smuggled goods within Bangladesh.
They are authorized to search, examine, and break open any locks, fixtures, or packages within the conveyance to carry out these duties.
When dealing with conveyances other than vessels or aircraft, they may use all lawful means to stop or prevent the escape of the conveyance, including firing upon it as a last resort.
Conveyance: Any conveyance, including vessels and aircraft, suspected of involvement in smuggling or carrying smuggled goods is subject to being stopped, searched, or compelled to land by customs authorities.
Owners or operators are legally required to stop immediately when signaled by authorized government vessels or aircraft, or face the risk of being chased or fired upon if they fail to comply.
Smuggling: This act forms the basis for the enforcement powers granted to customs officers to intervene against vehicles or vessels suspected of facilitating the illegal movement of goods.
Smuggled Goods: The transport of such goods within Bangladesh grants customs officers the legal authority to intercept and search any conveyance found to be carrying or intending to carry them.
Government: The government is authorized to designate specific authorities to signal vessels or aircraft to stop or land, and may employ government vessels or aircraft to enforce these directives through international signaling or the use of force.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Power to examine persons
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
165. Power to examine persons.- (1) The appropriate officer may, during the course of an inquiry in connection with the smuggling of any goods,-
(a) require any person to produce or deliver any document or thing to such officer,
(b) examine any person acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case.
(2) The appropriate officer shall exercise the powers in sub-section (1) only in relation to a person who is readily available or present before him and shall be subject to the same provisions as an officer-in-charge of a police-station is subject to under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), when investigating a offence.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer has the authority to conduct inquiries related to the smuggling of goods.
During such inquiries, the officer may require individuals to produce documents or objects and examine those familiar with the facts of the case.

The officer must exercise these examination powers only on persons present or readily available to them, operating under the same legal constraints as an officer-in-charge of a police station when investigating an offence.
Smuggling: The appropriate officer is empowered to initiate an inquiry whenever there is a connection to the smuggling of goods.
Person: Persons involved in a customs inquiry may be required to produce documents or things to the appropriate officer or be examined regarding the facts of the case.
These investigative powers are applicable only to individuals who are readily available or present before the appropriate officer.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: The procedures and legal standards governing an appropriate officer's investigation are subject to the same provisions as those applied to an officer-in-charge of a police station under this code.
Officer-in-charge of Police Station: The legal conduct and powers of the appropriate officer during an examination are benchmarked against the standards required of an officer-in-charge of a police station when performing investigations under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Seizure of things liable to confiscation
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
168. Seizure of things liable to confiscation.- (1) The appropriate officer may seize any goods liable to confiscation under this Act, and where it is not practicable to seize any such goods, he may serve on the owner of the goods or any person holding them in his possession or charge an order that he shall not remove, part with, or otherwise deal with the goods except with the previous permission of such officer.
(2) Where any goods are seized under sub-section (1) and no show cause notice in respect thereof is given under section 180 within two months of the seizure of the goods, the goods shall be returned to the person from whose possession they were seized:
Provided that the aforesaid period of two months may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, be extended by the 1[Commissioner of Customs] by a period not exceeding two months.
(3) The appropriate officer may seize any documents or things which in his opinion will be useful as evidence in any proceedings under this Act.
(4) The person from whose custody any documents are seized under sub-section (3) shall be entitled to make copies thereof or take extracts therefrom in the presence of an officer of customs.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer of customs is empowered to seize goods that are liable to confiscation under this Act.
When physical seizure is not practicable, the appropriate officer may issue a restrictive order preventing the owner or possessor from dealing with the goods without prior permission.
The appropriate officer is authorized to seize any documents or things deemed useful as evidence in legal proceedings conducted under this Act.
Seizure of Goods: Goods liable to confiscation may be seized by customs authorities, or if physical seizure is not possible, restricted through a formal order.
If a show cause notice is not issued within a specified timeframe following the seizure of goods, the goods must be returned to the person from whom they were seized.
The period for issuing a show cause notice after a seizure may be extended by the Commissioner of Customs for a limited duration, provided the reasons for the extension are recorded in writing.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to extend the period for issuing a show cause notice after the seizure of goods for an additional period, contingent upon recording the reasons in writing.
Documentary Evidence: Documents or things may be seized by an appropriate officer if they are considered useful as evidence for customs proceedings.
Persons from whose custody documents are seized retain the right to create copies or take extracts from those documents in the presence of a customs officer.
Person: A person in possession or charge of goods may be served with an order restricting the movement or disposal of those goods when physical seizure by customs is not feasible.
A person from whom goods were seized is entitled to their return if a formal show cause notice is not issued within the legally prescribed period.
A person from whom documents are seized for evidence is permitted to copy or extract information from them while supervised by a customs officer.

Person in Charge: A person in charge of goods being imported or exported by land must produce the required clearance orders upon the request of an appropriate officer of customs.
Imported Goods: Imported goods passing from a foreign frontier to an inland customs station via a prescribed route are exempted from the requirement to produce clearance orders.
National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to issue notifications in the official Gazette to exempt specific areas or goods of a certain description or value from these clearance production requirements.
Customs Clearance: The officer may demand the production of the order permitting inward clearance under section 83 or the order passing the bill of export under section 131.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Issue of show-cause notice before confiscation of goods or imposition of penalty

Confiscation of Goods: This clause requires that a show-cause notice must be issued to the owner of the goods before any order for their confiscation is passed under the Customs Act 1969.
The requirement for a show-cause notice does not apply if the owner of the goods admits the offence in writing and consents to the order without the issuance of such a notice.
Customs Penalty: Before any penalty is imposed on a person under the Customs Act 1969, they must be formally notified in writing of the grounds for the proposed action.
The person facing a penalty must be given a reasonable opportunity to make a written representation and to be heard personally or through an authorized representative.
The requirement to issue a show-cause notice prior to imposing a penalty is waived if the person concerned admits the offence in writing and requests that the order be passed without such notice.
Show Cause Notice: A show-cause notice acts as a mandatory procedural safeguard that informs an individual of the grounds for a proposed confiscation or penalty action.
The notice provides the recipient with a reasonable opportunity to respond in writing and to be heard, ensuring due process before any final administrative order is issued.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is responsible for specifying the reasonable time frame within which the person affected by a proposed customs action must submit their written representation.
Agent: The person against whom a customs action is proposed has the legal right to be heard personally or through a duly authorized agent during the show-cause process.

183. Levy of penalty for departure without authority or failure to bring-to.- (1) If any conveyance actually departs without a port clearance or permission in writing or, in the case of a vessel, after having failed to bring-to when required at any station appointed under section 14, the penalty to which the person-in-charge of such conveyance is liable may be adjudged by the appropriate officer of any customs-station, to which such conveyance proceeds, or in which it for the time being is.
(2) A certificate in respect of such departure or failure to bring-to when required, purporting to be signed by the appropriate officer of the customs-station from which the conveyance is stated to have so departed, shall be prima facie proof of the fact so stated.

Conveyance: A conveyance that departs without required port clearance or written permission, or a vessel that fails to bring-to as instructed at an appointed station, is subject to specific penalty provisions.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer at any customs station where the conveyance is found or proceeds has the authority to adjudge penalties against the person in charge for unauthorized departure or failure to bring-to.
A signed certificate issued by an officer at the customs station of departure serves as evidence regarding the occurrence of the unauthorized departure or failure to comply with instructions.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: The person in charge of a conveyance is held liable for penalties if the conveyance departs without proper authorization or fails to follow lawful instructions to bring-to at a station.
Burden of Proof: A certificate issued by the appropriate customs officer confirming a violation acts as evidence for the facts stated therein regarding the conveyance's departure or failure to bring-to.

(2) When any fine or penalty has been imposed in respect of any goods, the appropriate officer may detain any other goods belonging to the same owner pending payment of such fine or penalty.

Goods: Where a fine or penalty has been imposed or is under consideration in respect of specific goods, those goods may not be removed by the owner until the payment of the fine or penalty is satisfied.
Appropriate officers of customs are authorized to detain other goods belonging to the same owner as security for the payment of an outstanding fine or penalty imposed on any goods.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to detain goods belonging to an owner who has an unpaid fine or penalty in order to ensure the recovery of such amounts.
Customs Penalty: The law requires the satisfaction of fines or penalties as a condition for the release of goods involved in an offence and provides for the detention of other assets of the owner until such liabilities are discharged.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Deposit, pending appeal, of duty demanded or penalty levied
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
194. Deposit, pending appeal, of duty demanded or penalty levied.- (1) Any person desirous of appealing under section 193 5[or section 196A] against any decision or order relating to any duty demanded in respect of goods which have ceased to be under the control of customs authorities or to any penalty levied under this Act shall, at the time of filing his appeal or if he is so permitted by the appellate authority at any later stage before the consideration of the appeal, deposit with the appropriate officer 37[fifty per cent of the duty demanded or fifty per cent of the penalty imposed, or both, as the case may be]:
Provided that such person may, instead of depositing 38[the amount of the penalty as aforesaid] deposit only fifty per cent thereof and furnish a guarantee from a scheduled bank for the due payment of the balance:
Provided further that where, in any particular case, the appellate authority is of the opinion that the deposit of duty demanded or 39[penalty imposed] will cause undue hardship to the appellant, it may dispense with such deposit, either unconditionally or subject to such conditions as it may deem fit to impose.
(2) If, upon an appeal it is decided that the whole or any portion of the aforesaid duty or penalty was not leviable, the appropriate officer shall return to the appellant such amount or portion as the case may be.

Customs Authority: The customs authority maintains control over goods, and certain appeal processes regarding duty or penalties apply when goods have ceased to be under their custody.
Duty Payment: A person appealing a decision regarding demanded duties is generally required to deposit a specified percentage of the demanded amount with the appropriate officer, unless otherwise permitted by the appellate authority.
If an appeal results in a decision that the duty was not leviable, the appropriate officer is required to refund the amount paid by the appellant.
Customs Penalty: A person appealing against a levied penalty must deposit a specified percentage of the penalty amount, or may alternatively provide a bank guarantee for the balance under specific conditions.
The appellate authority has the discretion to waive the deposit requirement for penalties if it determines that payment would cause undue hardship to the appellant.
Upon a successful appeal where it is decided the penalty was not leviable, the appropriate officer shall refund the paid amount to the appellant.
Customs Appellate Tribunal: The appellate authority has the power to allow the deposit of duty or penalties at a later stage before the appeal is considered and may dispense with the deposit requirement entirely if deemed necessary to avoid undue hardship.
Scheduled Bank: An appellant may provide a guarantee from a scheduled bank to cover the balance of a penalty amount instead of depositing the full required sum.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is responsible for receiving the required deposits of duty or penalties from the appellant and for processing refunds if an appeal is successful.

Public Demands Recovery Act 1913: This act serves as the legal basis for the appointment of certificate officers tasked with recovering outstanding government dues as a public demand or arrear of land revenue.

32. Untrue statement, error, etc.- (1) If any person, in connection with any matter of customs,-

(3) Where, by reason of any inadvertence, error or misconstruction, any duty or charge 1[amounting to not less than one thousand taka] has not been levied or has been short-levied or has been erroneously refunded, the person liable to pay any amount on that account shall be served with a notice within 2[three years] of the relevant date requiring him to show cause why he should not pay the amount specified in the notice.

Vessel: A vessel is subject to a mandatory entry outward process, requiring the master to submit a written application to the appropriate officer and obtain an order for entry before any export goods can be loaded.
Vessel Master: The master of a vessel is responsible for submitting a formal written application for entry outwards to the appropriate officer to facilitate the legal loading of export goods.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is the authority responsible for receiving written applications and issuing the necessary orders for the entry of vessels or authorization for the loading of other conveyances.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: For conveyances other than vessels, the person in charge must submit a written application for loading authorization to the appropriate officer to ensure legal compliance before loading goods.
National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to prescribe the specific particulars that must be included in applications for vessel entry or conveyance loading authorization under this section.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: No vessel to depart without port-clearance
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
51. No vessel to depart without port-clearance.- (1) No vessel, whether laden or in ballast, shall depart from any customs-port until a port-clearance has been granted by the appropriate officer.
(2) No pilot shall take charge of any vessel proceeding to sea, unless the master of such vessel produces a port-clearance.

Vessel: No vessel, whether carrying cargo or in ballast, is permitted to leave a customs port without first obtaining formal port clearance.
Customs Port: A customs port serves as the location from which vessels must obtain official clearance before their departure.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate customs officer is the authority responsible for granting the necessary port clearance to a vessel.
Pilot: A pilot is prohibited from taking charge of a vessel heading out to sea unless the master of that vessel presents a valid port clearance.
Master: The master of a vessel is required to produce a port clearance before a pilot can take charge of the vessel for its departure to sea.
Port Clearance: Port clearance acts as the mandatory legal authorization that must be granted by an appropriate customs officer and produced by the vessel master before a vessel can lawfully depart from a port.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: No conveyance other than vessel to leave without permission
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text: 52. No conveyance other than vessel to leave without permission.- No conveyance other than a vessel shall depart from a land customs-station or customs-airport until a written permission to that effect has been granted by the appropriate officer.

Conveyance: Any conveyance, excluding a vessel, is prohibited from leaving a land customs station or customs airport without first obtaining written permission from the appropriate customs officer.
Customs Station: Departures of conveyances other than vessels from land customs stations are subject to mandatory written authorization from customs authorities.
Customs Airport: Departures of conveyances other than vessels from customs airports are subject to mandatory written authorization from customs authorities.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is responsible for granting the formal written permission required before a non-vessel conveyance may depart from a land customs station or customs airport.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Application for port-clearance of vessels
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
53. Application for port-clearance of vessels.- (1) Every application for port-clearance Shall be made by the master of a vessel at least twenty-four hours before the intended departure of the vessel:
Provided that the 1[Commissioner of Customs] or an officer authorised by him in this behalf may for special reasons to be recorded allow a shorter period for the delivery of the said application2[:]
3[Provided further that when the master is a registered user, he may make the application under this sub-section by transmitting it to the Customs computer system, and an application so transmitted shall be deemed to have been duly signed by him.]
(2) The master shall, at the time of applying for port-clearance,-
(a) deliver to the appropriate officer an export manifest in duplicate in such form as may from time to time be prescribed by the Board signed by such master specifying all goods to be exported in the vessel and showing separately all goods and stores entered in the import manifest, and not landed or consumed on board or transhipped;
(b) deliver to the appropriate officer such bills of export or other documents as such officer acting under the general instructions of the 1[Commissioner of Customs] requires; and
(c) answer such questions respecting the departure and destination of the vessel as are put to him by the appropriate officer2[:
Provided that if the master is a registered user, he may transmit to the Customs computer system the export manifest and other documents specified at clauses (b) and (c) and the documents so transmitted shall be deemed to have been signed by him for the purposes of this section.]
(3) The provisions of section 45, relating to the amendment of import manifest shall, mutatis mutandis, apply also to export manifest delivered under this section or under section 54.

Port Clearance: The master of a vessel is required to submit an application for port clearance at least twenty-four hours before the vessel's intended departure. The Commissioner of Customs or an authorized officer may permit a shorter application period under special recorded circumstances.
Master: The master is responsible for applying for port clearance, delivering necessary documentation such as the export manifest and bills of export, and answering inquiries regarding the vessel's departure and destination. When acting as a registered user, the master may fulfill these requirements by transmitting documents to the customs computer system.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to approve a reduced timeframe for port clearance applications and provides general instructions for the documentation required during the clearance process.
Export Manifest: The master must deliver an export manifest in duplicate, which specifies all goods to be exported and details items carried over from the import manifest that remain on board. The document must follow the prescribed form and be signed by the master, or transmitted electronically if the master is a registered user.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer receives the export manifest, bills of export, and other required documents, and has the authority to examine the master regarding the vessel's departure and destination.
Registered User: A master who is a registered user may submit applications, export manifests, and other required documents via the customs computer system, with such transmissions legally deemed as signed by the master.
Customs Computerised Entry Processing Sy: The customs computer system serves as the digital platform for registered users to transmit export manifests and other clearance documents, substituting for physical document submission.

Export Manifest: items carried over from the import manifest

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Conveyances other than vessels to deliver documents and answer question before departure
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
54. Conveyances other than vessels to deliver documents and answer question before departure.- The person-in-charge of a conveyance other than a vessel or his duly authorised agent shall-
(a) deliver to the appropriate officer an export manifest in duplicate in such form as may from time to time be prescribed by the Board signed by such person-in-charge or the agent specifying all goods or stores entered in the import manifest, and not landed or transhipped or consumed on board the conveyance;
(b) deliver to the appropriate officer such bills of export or other documents as such officer acting under the general instructions of the 1[Commissioner of Customs] requires; and
(c) answer such questions respecting the departure and destination of the conveyance as are put to him by the appropriate officer.

Person in Charge of Conveyance: The person in charge of a conveyance, other than a vessel, or their authorized agent is legally obligated to perform specific procedural tasks before the departure of the conveyance.

They must provide the appropriate officer with an export manifest in the prescribed form, submit necessary bills of export or other required documentation, and respond to inquiries regarding the conveyance's departure and destination.
Agent: An agent may act on behalf of the person in charge of a conveyance to fulfill legal requirements for document delivery and manifest submission before departure.
Export Manifest: The person in charge of a conveyance must deliver an export manifest in duplicate to the appropriate officer.
This document must be signed and detail all goods or stores that were included in the import manifest but were not landed, transhipped, or consumed during the transit.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is the designated authority to receive the export manifest, bills of export, and other required documents from the person in charge of the conveyance.
They are also authorized to question the person in charge regarding the conveyance's departure and destination.
National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to prescribe the form for the export manifest that must be submitted by the person in charge of the conveyance.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs provides the general instructions under which the appropriate officer requires the submission of specific bills of export and additional documentation.

Person in Charge of Conveyance: person in charge of a conveyance
Agent: person in charge of a conveyance
Appropriate Officer of Customs: person in charge of the conveyance
National Board of Revenue: person in charge of the conveyance

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Power to refuse port-clearance to vessels or permission for departure to other conveyance

Port Clearance: The appropriate officer of customs has the authority to refuse port clearance to a vessel or permission for departure to other conveyances until all relevant legal requirements and payments are satisfied.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to demand security, guarantees, or deposits to ensure the payment of dues, taxes, and penalties before granting departure permission to a conveyance.
The officer may require the unloading of goods exported in violation of the law or, if unloading is impractical, demand an undertaking and security for bringing the goods back to Bangladesh.
Conveyance: Departure permission for any conveyance may be withheld until all port dues, charges, and penalties applicable to the conveyance or its person-in-charge have been settled.
Vessel: Port clearance for a vessel may be withheld until all applicable port dues, penalties, and taxes related to the vessel, its master, or its cargo have been paid or secured.
Agent: An agent may provide a written declaration assuming liability for specific penalties and furnish security, thereby becoming responsible for such discharge.
An agent may provide a written declaration assuming responsibility for claims regarding damage or short delivery of imported goods, becoming legally bound to discharge those claims.
Person in Charge: The person-in-charge of a conveyance is responsible for the payment of all dues, taxes, and penalties related to the conveyance or its cargo before departure is permitted.
Export Goods: If export goods are loaded without paying required taxes or duties, or in violation of law, they must be unloaded or the agent must provide an undertaking and security to bring the goods back to Bangladesh.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Grant of port-clearance or permission for departure
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text: 56. Grant of port-clearance or permission for departure.- When the appropriate officer is satisfied that the provisions of this Chapter relating to the departure of conveyances have been duly complied with, he shall grant a port- clearance to the master of the vessel or a written permission for departure to the person-in-charge of any other conveyance and shall return at the same time to such master or person-in-charge one copy of the manifest duly countersigned by the appropriate officer.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The officer is responsible for verifying that all legal requirements concerning the departure of a conveyance have been satisfied before authorizing its departure.
Port Clearance: This document is granted to the master of a vessel by the appropriate officer once all departure requirements are met.
Departure Permission: This written authorization is issued to the person-in-charge of a conveyance, other than a vessel, upon the fulfillment of all necessary departure formalities.
Master of the Vessel: The master must receive port clearance and a countersigned copy of the manifest from the appropriate officer before the vessel is permitted to depart.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: This person must obtain written permission for departure from the appropriate officer, along with a countersigned copy of the manifest, after ensuring all regulatory compliance for departure.
Manifest: A copy of the manifest must be countersigned by the appropriate officer and returned to the master or person-in-charge of the conveyance upon the granting of departure permission.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Grant of port-clearance or permission for departure on security of agent
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text: 57. Grant of port-clearance or permission for departure on security of agent.- Notwithstanding anything contained in section 55 or section 56 and subject to rules, the appropriate officer may grant a port-clearance in respect of a vessel or permission for departure in respect of any other conveyance, if the agent furnishes such security as such officer deems sufficient for duly delivering within ten days from the date of such grant, the export manifest and other documents specified in section 53 or section 54, as the case may be.

Port Clearance: The appropriate officer of customs may grant port clearance to a vessel despite standard requirements if the agent provides adequate security for the timely delivery of required export documents.
Departure Permission: The appropriate officer of customs may grant permission for the departure of a conveyance, other than a vessel, provided the agent furnishes sufficient security to ensure the later submission of mandatory export manifests and associated documents.
Agent: The agent is responsible for providing financial security as deemed sufficient by the appropriate officer of customs to secure the delivery of export documents within a specified period following the grant of clearance or departure permission.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to exercise discretion in accepting security from an agent to facilitate the clearance of vessels or the departure of conveyances.
Export Manifest: Agents must ensure the delivery of the export manifest within ten days from the date of receiving port clearance or departure permission.
Security Bond: A security bond or equivalent security must be furnished by the agent to guarantee the timely submission of required export documents to customs authorities.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Power to cancel port-clearance or permission for departure
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
58. Power to cancel port-clearance or permission for departure.- (1) For the purpose of securing compliance with any provision of this Act or the rules or any other law, the appropriate officer may at any time, while the vessel is within the limits of any port or any other conveyance is within the limits of any station or airport or within 1[Bangladesh] territory, demand the return of port- clearance or the written permission for departure, as the case may be.
(2) Any such demand may be made in writing or may be communicated to the person-in-charge of the conveyance by wireless, and if made in writing it may be served-
(a) by delivery to the person-in-charge or his agent personally; or
(b) by leaving it at the last known place of abode of such person or agent; or
(c) by leaving it on board the conveyance with the person appearing to be in charge or command thereof.
(3) Where a demand for the return of a port-clearance or of a permission for departure is made as aforesaid, the port-clearance or permission shall forthwith become void.

Port Clearance: The appropriate officer may demand the return of a port clearance for the purpose of securing compliance with the Customs Act or other relevant laws while a vessel is within port limits or Bangladesh territory.
A port clearance becomes immediately void once a valid demand for its return has been made by the appropriate officer.
Departure Permission: The appropriate officer is empowered to demand the return of written permission for departure from a conveyance while it is located within a customs station, airport, or Bangladeshi territory.
Once a formal demand for the return of a departure permission is issued, the document is legally rendered void.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is authorized to secure legal compliance by demanding the return of port clearance or departure permission from conveyances located within their jurisdiction.
The officer may issue these demands in writing or via wireless communication to the person in charge of the conveyance.
Conveyance: When located within the limits of a station, airport, or Bangladeshi territory, a conveyance is subject to the authority of customs officers regarding the cancellation of departure permissions.
Demands for the return of clearance documents may be served by leaving the notice on board the conveyance with the person currently in command.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: The person in charge of a conveyance is the recipient of any demand for the return of clearance or departure permissions, which may be delivered personally, left at their last known residence, or communicated via wireless.
They are responsible for complying with the demand, following which their current clearance or departure permission becomes void.
Agent: A written demand for the return of port clearance or departure permission may be legally served by delivering the notice to the agent of the person in charge of the conveyance.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: person in charge of the conveyance
Person in Charge of Conveyance: person in charge of a conveyance
Agent: person in charge of the conveyance

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Power to depute officers of customs to board conveyances
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text: 60. Power to depute officers of customs to board conveyances.- At any time while a conveyance is in a customs-station or is proceeding towards such station, the appropriate officer may depute one or more officers of customs to board the conveyance, and every officer so deputed shall remain on board such conveyance for such time as the appropriate officer may consider necessary.

Conveyance: A customs officer has the authority to board a conveyance at any time while it is located within a customs station or is currently traveling towards one.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to depute other officers of customs to board a conveyance and determines the required duration for those officers to remain on board.
Officer of Customs: These officers may be deputed by an appropriate officer to board a conveyance and must remain on board for the duration deemed necessary by the appropriate officer.
Customs Station: The power to board a conveyance applies when the vessel or vehicle is located at or moving towards a customs-station.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Officers' powers of access, etc
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
62. Officers' powers of access, etc.- (1) Every officer deputed as aforesaid shall have free access to every part of the conveyance and may-
(a) cause any goods to be marked before they are unloaded from that conveyance;
(b) lock up, seal, mark or otherwise secure any goods carried in the conveyance or any place or container in which they are carried; or
(c) fasten down any hatchway or entrance to the hold.
(2) If any box, place or closed receptacle in any such conveyance be locked, and the key be withheld, such officer shall report the same to the appropriate officer, who may thereupon issue to the officer on board the conveyance or to any other officer under his authority, a written order for search.
(3) On production of such order, the officer empowered thereunder may require that any such box, place or closed receptacle be opened in his presence; and if it be not opened upon his requisition, he may break open the same.

Officer of Customs: These officers are granted the authority to access any part of a conveyance for the performance of their duties.
They are empowered to mark, lock, seal, or secure goods and containers, and to fasten hatchways or entrances to holds to ensure compliance.
Conveyance: A conveyance is subject to the authority of customs officers who have the power to access its various parts and secure cargo or entry points.
When keys to locked areas or receptacles on a conveyance are withheld, customs officers may obtain and execute written search orders to force access if necessary.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer acts as the authorizing authority who receives reports regarding locked receptacles on a conveyance and may issue written orders for their search.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Goods not to be loaded or unloaded or water-borne except in presence of officer
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text: 64. Goods not to be loaded or unloaded or water-borne except in presence of officer.- Save where general permission is given under section 67 or with permission in writing of the appropriate officer, no goods other than passengers’ baggage or ballast urgently required to be loaded for the vessel's safety, shall be shipped or water-borne to be shipped or discharged from any vessel, in any customs-port, nor any goods except passenger’ baggage shall be loaded in or unloaded from any conveyance other than a vessel at any land customs-station or customs-airport except in the presence of an officer of customs.

Goods: The loading, unloading, or movement of goods for shipment is generally prohibited in customs-ports, land customs-stations, or customs-airports unless conducted in the presence of an officer of customs.
Exceptions to this requirement include passenger baggage and ballast that is urgently needed for the safety of a vessel.
Officer of Customs: The presence of an officer of customs is mandatory for the loading or unloading of goods at customs-ports, land customs-stations, and customs-airports, unless specific written permission is granted by an appropriate officer or general permission is provided under the relevant section of the Act.
Vessel: The loading or discharging of goods from any vessel in a customs-port must occur in the presence of an officer of customs, except when goods consist of passenger baggage or safety-critical ballast.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to grant written permission for the loading or unloading of goods in circumstances where the general presence of a customs officer is otherwise required.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Goods not to be loaded or unloaded or passed on certain days or at certain times
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
65. Goods not to be loaded or unloaded or passed on certain days or at certain times.- Except with the permission of the appropriate officer and on payment of such fees as may be prescribed by the Board no goods, other than passengers’ baggage or mail bags, shall in any customs-port be discharged, or be shipped or water-borne to be shipped or shall be loaded or unloaded or passed at any land customs-station or customs-airport-
(a) on any public holiday within the meaning of the section 25 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (XXVI of 1881) or on any day on which the discharge or shipping of cargo at customs-port or loading, unloading, passage or delivery of cargo at any land customs-station or customs-airport, as the case may be, is prohibited by the Board by notification in the official Gazette; or
(b) on any day except between such hours as the Board may, from time to time, by like notification, appoint.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The loading, unloading, or passage of goods outside of permitted times and days requires the specific permission of the appropriate officer of customs.
Goods: Except for passengers' baggage and mail bags, the loading, unloading, or passage of goods is restricted at customs ports, land customs stations, and customs airports during public holidays or times not appointed by the Board.
Passenger Baggage: Passenger baggage is excluded from the general restrictions on loading, unloading, and passage of goods during restricted days or hours.
Mail Bags: Mail bags are excluded from the general restrictions on loading, unloading, and passage of goods during restricted days or hours.
National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to prescribe fees for loading or unloading activities during restricted times and to issue notifications in the official Gazette prohibiting such activities on specific days or limiting them to certain hours.
Negotiable Instruments Act 1881: This Act provides the legal definition of public holidays, which serves as a criteria for determining restricted days for customs operations.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Goods not to be loaded or unloaded except at approved places
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text: 66. Goods not to be loaded or unloaded except at approved places.- Save where general permission is given under section 67 or with permission in writing of the appropriate officer, no imported goods shall be unloaded or goods for export loaded at any place other than a place duly approved under clause (b) of section 10 for the unloading or loading of such goods.

Imported Goods: Imported goods must not be unloaded at any location other than one that has been officially approved for such activities.
Export Goods: Goods intended for export must only be loaded at a place that has been duly approved for this purpose.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer of customs has the authority to grant written permission for the loading or unloading of goods at locations other than those officially approved.
Customs Procedure for Loading Goods: Loading and unloading activities are restricted to approved places unless a general permission is granted under section 67 or specific written permission is obtained from the appropriate officer.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Discharge of goods by conveyances other than vessels
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text: 74. Discharge of goods by conveyances other than vessels.- When on arrival of a conveyance other than a vessel at a land customs-station or customs- airport the person-in-charge of such conveyance has delivered the import manifest under section 44 and the documents required under section 48, he shall forthwith take the conveyance or cause it to be taken to the examination station at the land customs-station or customs-airport and remove or cause to be removed all goods carried in such conveyance to the custom-house in the presence of the appropriate officer or some person duly authorised by him in that behalf.

Conveyance: Upon arrival at a customs station or customs airport, the person in charge must move the conveyance to the designated examination station after fulfilling initial manifest and documentation requirements.
Customs Station: The person in charge of a conveyance is required to take the vehicle to the examination station located at the customs station for the purpose of discharging goods.
Customs Airport: Upon arrival, the person in charge must proceed to the examination station at the customs airport to facilitate the removal and discharge of goods.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: Following the delivery of the import manifest and required documents, this person must ensure the conveyance is moved to the examination station and that all goods are transferred to the custom house under official supervision.
Import Manifest: The delivery of this document is a mandatory prerequisite for the person in charge to proceed with the movement of the conveyance and the discharge of goods.
Customs Documents: The person in charge must submit all required documents under the relevant section of the Customs Act 1969 before initiating the discharge of goods.
Customs House: Goods carried by a conveyance must be removed and transported to this location in the presence of an appropriate officer or an authorized person.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The removal of goods from a conveyance to the custom house must be conducted in the presence of this officer or a person duly authorized by them.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Imported goods not to be unloaded unless entered in the import manifest
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
75. Imported goods not to be unloaded unless entered in the import manifest.- (1) No imported goods required to be shown in the import manifest shall, except with the permission of the appropriate officer, be unloaded from any conveyance at any customs-station unless they are specified in the import manifest or amended or supplementary import manifest for being unloaded at that customs-station.
(2) Nothing in the section shall apply to the unloading of the baggage accompanying a passenger or a member or a crew or mail bags.

Imported Goods: Imported goods that are required to be declared in an import manifest cannot be unloaded from a conveyance at a customs-station unless they are explicitly listed in the import manifest or its approved amendments.
Unloading of these goods without being specified in the manifest is prohibited unless the appropriate officer of customs grants specific permission.
Import Manifest: The import manifest serves as the legal record that must specify the goods intended to be unloaded at a customs-station.
Provisions allow for the submission of amended or supplementary import manifests to include goods for unloading.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer of customs holds the authority to grant permission for the unloading of imported goods that might otherwise not be permitted to be unloaded.
Conveyance: The unloading of imported goods from any conveyance at a customs-station is strictly regulated to ensure all items are entered in the import manifest.
Customs Station: The regulations concerning the mandatory inclusion of goods in an import manifest apply to all unloading activities occurring at a customs-station.
Baggage: The requirement to list goods in an import manifest before unloading does not apply to the baggage accompanying a passenger or a member of the crew.
Mail Bags: Mail bags are exempt from the requirement to be entered in the import manifest before they are unloaded at a customs-station.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Procedure in respect of goods not unloaded by vessels within time allowed
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
76. Procedure in respect of goods not unloaded by vessels within time allowed.- (1) (a) If any goods imported by a vessel (except such as have been shown in the import manifest as not to be unloaded) are not unloaded within such period as is specified in the bill of lading or if no period is so specified, within such number of the working days, not exceeding fifteen, after entry of the vessel as the Board may from time to time by notification in the official Gazette appoint, or
(b) if the cargo of any vessel, excepting a small quantity of goods, has been discharged before the expiration of the period so specified or appointed, the master of such vessel or, on this application, the appropriate officer may then carry such goods to the custom-house, there to remain for entry.
1[(2) The appropriate officer shall thereupon take charge of, and grant receipt for, such goods; and if notice in writing has been given by the master or the agent of the vessel to the appropriate officer that goods are to remain subject to a lien for freight, primage, general average demurrage, container detention charges, dead-freight, terminal handling charges, container service charge or other charges of a stated amount, the appropriate officer shall hold such goods until he receives notice in writing that the said charges have been paid.]

Imported Goods: These are goods imported by a vessel that remain unloaded after the time limit specified in the bill of lading or the period appointed by the Board.
The appropriate officer may move these goods to the custom-house for entry if they are not unloaded within the allowed timeframe, or if the majority of the cargo has been discharged early.
Vessel: The master of the vessel is responsible for ensuring goods are unloaded within the specified period or timeframe.
The master or agent may notify the appropriate officer that goods are subject to a lien for various outstanding charges, such as freight, demurrage, or container-related fees.
Bill of Lading: This document specifies the period within which imported goods must be unloaded from the vessel.
National Board of Revenue: The Board is authorized to notify, through the official Gazette, the maximum number of working days allowed for unloading goods after a vessel has entered.
Customs House: Goods that are not unloaded within the allowed time may be carried to the custom-house to be held until entry is processed.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is authorized to take charge of and issue a receipt for goods that have not been unloaded within the required time.
The officer must hold goods subject to a notified lien for freight and other listed charges until they receive written confirmation that these charges have been paid.
Agent: The agent of the vessel may provide written notice to the appropriate officer regarding liens on goods for unpaid charges, such as freight, demurrage, or terminal handling fees.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Power to land small parcels and hold unclaimed parcels
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
77. Power to land small parcels and hold unclaimed parcels.- (1) At any time after the arrival of any vessel, the appropriate officer may, with the consent of the master of such vessel, cause any small package or parcel of goods to be carried to the custom-house there to remain for entry in-charge of the officers of customs, during the remainder of the working days allowed under this Act for the landing of such package or parcel.
(2) In any package or parcel so carried to the custom-house remains unclaimed on the expiration of the number of working days so allowed for its unloading or at the time of the clearance outwards of the vessel from which it was unloaded, the master of such vessel may give such notice as is provided in section 76, and the officer-in-charge of the custom-house shall thereupon hold such package or parcel as provided in that section.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to arrange for the transfer of small packages or parcels from an arriving vessel to the custom-house with the consent of the vessel master.
Vessel: Upon arrival of a vessel, the appropriate officer may move small parcels or packages to the custom-house for entry.
Master of the Vessel: The master must provide consent for the removal of small parcels to the custom-house and is authorized to provide notice regarding unclaimed goods once the allowed unloading period or vessel clearance time has passed.
Customs House: The custom-house serves as the designated facility for holding small packages or parcels pending entry or further claim by the owner.
Officer of Customs: These officers are responsible for the custody of goods carried to the custom-house for the duration of the allowed working days.
Unclaimed Cargo: Parcels remaining at the custom-house after the allowed timeframe or upon the vessel's departure are subject to hold procedures as specified in the Act.

static_replicated_objects.clause_title: Power to permit immediate discharge
static_replicated_objects.resolved_text:
78. Power to permit immediate discharge.- (1) Notwithstanding anything contended in sections 74, 76 and 77, the appropriate officer in any customs-station to which the Board, by notification in the official Gazette, declares this section to apply, may permit the master of any vessel immediately on receipt of an order under section 47 or a special pass under section 49, or the person-in-charge of a conveyance other than a vessel on receipt of the import manifest to discharge the goods imported by such conveyance, or any portion thereof, into the custody of his agent, if he be willing to receive the same, for the purpose of unloading the same forthwith-
(a) at the custom-house, or at any specified landing-place or wharf; or
(b) at any landing-place or wharf belonging to the port commissioners, port trust, railways or other public body or company; or
(c) for giving it in the custody of such person as may be approved by the 2[Commissioner of Customs].
(2) Any agent so receiving such cargo or portion shall be bound to discharge all claims for damage or short delivery which may be established in respect of the same by the owner thereof, and shall be entitled to recover from such owner his charges for service rendered, but not for commission or the like, where any agent for the unloading of such cargo or portion has been previously appointed by the owner and such appointment is unrevoked 1[:
Provide that no agent so receiving such cargo or portion shall cause it to be removed or otherwise dealt with except in accordance with the written order of the appropriate officer.]
(3) The appropriate officer shall take charge of all goods discharged under clause (a) of sub-section (1) and otherwise proceed in relation thereto as provided in section 76 and 82.
(4) 2[A public body or company or port authority or airlines or] person at whose landing- place or wharf or place of storage any goods are discharged under clause (b) or clause (c) of sub-section (1) shall not permit the same to be removed or otherwise dealt with except in accordance with the order in writing of the appropriate officer.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer has the authority to permit the immediate discharge of goods from a vessel or conveyance into the custody of an agent, provided the customs-station has been declared applicable for this section by the Board.

This officer is responsible for managing the custody of goods discharged at custom-houses and ensuring that goods discharged at authorized landing places or warehouses are not removed or dealt with without written authorization.
The officer must proceed with the handling of discharged goods in accordance with the prescribed sections of the Customs Act 1969.
National Board of Revenue: The Board holds the power to designate specific customs-stations where the provision for immediate discharge of goods may be applied through a notification in the official Gazette.
Master of the Vessel: The master of a vessel may be permitted to immediately discharge imported goods upon receiving a valid arrival order or a special pass.
Person in Charge of Conveyance: The person in charge of a conveyance other than a vessel is authorized to discharge imported goods upon receipt of the import manifest, subject to the permission of the appropriate officer.
Agent: An agent may receive imported goods for immediate discharge if they are willing to do so, assuming legal responsibility for claims related to damage or short delivery.

The agent is entitled to recover service charges from the owner of the goods but is prohibited from removing or dealing with the cargo except as permitted by the written order of the appropriate officer.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs is authorized to approve the specific persons permitted to hold goods in custody under the immediate discharge provisions.
Port Authority: Port authorities, public bodies, or companies providing landing places or storage are prohibited from allowing the removal or handling of discharged goods without the written order of the appropriate officer.
Imported Goods: Imported goods may be discharged immediately into the custody of an agent at approved locations such as custom-houses, wharves, or other public body storage facilities to facilitate prompt unloading.

Person in Charge of Conveyance: person in charge of a conveyance

79. Entry for home-consumption or warehousing.- (1) The owner of any imported goods shall make entry of such goods for home-consumption or warehousing or for any other approved purpose by delivering to the appropriate officer a bill of entry thereof in such form and manner and containing such particulars as the Board may direct:
Provided that, if the owner makes and subscribes a declaration before the appropriate officer to the effect that he is unable, for want of 3[such information as is essential for submitting a bill of entry], then the said officer shall permit him, previous to the entry thereof, to examine the goods in the presence of an officer of customs or to deposit such goods in a public warehouse appointed under section 12 without warehousing the same, pending the production of such information.
4[(1A) The Commissioner of Customs may within the period specified in sub-section (2) require the owner who has delivered or transmitted a bill of entry in electronic form to submit to the appropriate officer a paper bill of entry duly signed by the owner or his authorized agent, containing such information and documents as the said Commissioner may specify;]
5[(2) A bill of entry under sub-section (1) may be presented and the goods be cleared at any time within 20[thirty] days of the date of unloading thereof at a customs-port or a land customs-station or customs-inland container depot or 21[within twenty one days of] the date of unloading thereof at a customs- airport or within such extended period as the 6[Commissioner of Customs] may deem fit:
7[Provided that the Commissioner of Customs may permit a bill of entry to be presented even before the delivery of the manifest if the vessel or the aircraft by which the goods have been shipped for importation into Bangladesh is expected to arrive within thirty days from the date of such presentation.]
(3) If the 6[Commissioner of Customs] is satisfied that the rate of customs-duty is not adversely affected and that there was no intention to defraud, he may in exceptional circumstances and for reasons to be recorded in writing permit substitution of a bill of entry for home-consumption for a bill of entry for warehousing or vice versa.

Imported Goods: The owner of imported goods is required to submit a bill of entry for the purposes of home-consumption, warehousing, or other approved purposes.

In cases where essential information for a bill of entry is missing, the owner may be permitted to examine the goods or deposit them in a public warehouse pending the submission of the required details.
Bill of Entry: A bill of entry must be presented to the appropriate officer in a form and manner directed by the National Board of Revenue.
Electronic bills of entry may be subject to a request from the Commissioner of Customs for a signed paper version containing specific supporting information and documents.

The bill of entry generally must be presented within a specified timeframe following the unloading of goods at a customs-port, land customs-station, customs-inland container depot, or customs-airport, though extensions may be granted.
Under certain conditions, the Commissioner of Customs may allow a bill of entry to be presented prior to the delivery of the manifest.

A substitution between a bill of entry for home-consumption and one for warehousing may be permitted by the Commissioner of Customs in exceptional circumstances if there is no intention to defraud and customs-duty rates are not negatively impacted.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is responsible for receiving the bill of entry and supervising the examination of goods when necessary.
The appropriate officer may permit the deposit of goods into a public warehouse if the owner lacks the information required for a full entry.
National Board of Revenue: The Board is empowered to direct the form, manner, and required particulars for the submission of a bill of entry.
Public Warehouse: Goods may be deposited in a public warehouse pending the availability of information required for a formal bill of entry.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner has the authority to request a paper version of an electronic bill of entry and grant extensions for the presentation of such documents.
The Commissioner may permit the presentation of a bill of entry before the delivery of a manifest if the vessel or aircraft is expected to arrive within a defined period.

The Commissioner may authorize the substitution of a bill of entry for home-consumption with one for warehousing, or vice versa, provided specific conditions regarding duty rates and intent are satisfied.
Authorized Representative: An authorized agent may be required to sign and submit a paper bill of entry on behalf of the owner when requested by the Commissioner of Customs.
